extracted.intended_audience: trademark attorneys, applicants, USPTO/TTAB examiners, and appellate counsel in U.S. trademark matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria for determining whether a proposed trademark/service mark is generic under U.S. law, including burden of proof, types of admissible evidence, evaluation of surveys and declarations, and appellate review standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genericness is a question of fact and a bar to registration
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic term cannot be registered as a trademark, for generic terms by definition are incapable of indicating source; a generic term is the common name for the genus of goods or services being sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the designation is the common name for the genus of goods/services. If the term is generic, registration must be refused. Case citations: Merrill Lynch; H. Marvin Ginn Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on the PTO to establish genericness by clear evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent and Trademark Office bears the burden of establishing that a proposed mark is generic, and must demonstrate generic status by clear evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examining attorneys must prove genericness by clear and convincing evidence. (TMPEP 1209.01(c)(i); In re Merrill Lynch; McCarthy commentary.) The heightened burden affects evaluation of the record on review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of appellate review: legal conclusions plenary, facts for substantial evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulings of the PTO tribunals are reviewed under the Administrative Procedure Act: plenary review for TTAB legal conclusions, and review of factual findings for whether they are arbitrary, capricious, or unsupported by substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On appellate review of genericness, determine if substantial evidence on the entirety of the record supports the Board's factual findings; when the fact requires 'clear evidence', that heightened burden must be considered in the sufficiency analysis. (Dickinson v. Zurko; Bridgestone/Firestone; Anderson v. Liberty Lobby.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer perception controls placement on the generic-descriptive-suggestive-arbitrary-fanciful continuum
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a term is entitled to trademark status turns on how the mark is understood by the purchasing public; there is no fixed boundary between categories and each word must be considered in its circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on consumer understanding of the term in context; examine how prospective customers perceive the designation (In re Montrachet; K-T Zoe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of components vs. whole in composite/domain-name marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the composite (e.g., HOTELS.COM) communicates more than the common meanings of its individual components; the addition of a '.com' suffix does not automatically create a registrable mark if the generic component still names the genus of services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether the combination produces a new meaning or simply conveys the common meanings of components (e.g., Reed Elsevier: LAWYERS.COM; Gould Paper: SCREENWIPE). Domain suffixes do not inherently negate genericness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dictionary, encyclopedic, and thesaurus definitions as evidence of genericness
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionaries, encyclopedias, and thesauri definitions of component words (and of suffixes like '.com') are admissible evidence that terms name the services provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and cite standard definitions showing the ordinary meaning (the TTAB relied on American Heritage Dictionary definitions of 'hotel' and '.com').

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party usage and competitor/domain name evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Printouts and examples of third-party websites and domain names that use the same term (or the term with '.com') to identify hotel information/reservation services support a finding of genericness and show competitive need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey third-party domain names, website descriptions, and industry usage to show the term is used generically (e.g., all-hotels.com, web-hotels.com, my-discount-hotels.com). Evidence that many competitors use the term supports a prima facie case of genericness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive need as indicia of genericness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that others need to use the term in their domain names/trademarks to describe their services supports the conclusion that the term denotes the genus and is generic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document instances where competitors must use the term descriptively; the TTAB included competitive need among factors supporting genericness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and probative value of declarations/rebuttal statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations from customers, vendors, or competitors asserting a term is not generic can be given limited weight if they are identical form declarations without explanation of basis or demonstration of how the public perceives the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations should be individual, explain the declarant's basis for perception, and avoid boilerplate form language; identical form declarations risk being discounted (TTAB criticized 64 identical declarations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey evidence must be properly designed and targeted to consumer perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey evidence is evaluated for probative value based on survey design, the specific questions asked, and the surveyor's experience; surveys must address how consumers perceive the designation's meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys that 'teach' respondents distinctions (e.g., brand vs. common name) or that frame questions in a way that biases responses can be criticized; design must directly probe consumer perception of the term in its marketplace context (TTAB criticized the DuPont 'Teflon' methodology survey for skewing results). Cite Stuhlbarg and McCarthy §12:17.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired distinctiveness (Section 2(f)) vs. genericness
rubrics_metrics.description: While a merely descriptive term may acquire distinctiveness and be registrable under Section 2(f), acquired distinctiveness does not overcome a finding that a term is generic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a mark is found merely descriptive, evidence of secondary meaning (length/use/advertising/sales) may support registration; but a showing of secondary meaning cannot register a generic term. Note: TTAB may consider Section 2(f) evidence in the alternative, but genericness is dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context of use is important but not dispositive if component meanings remain dominant
rubrics_metrics.description: Context — including how the term is used on websites, in advertising, and in consumer interactions — is evidence of perception, but context will not convert a generic component into a source-indicating mark if the composite communicates the ordinary meanings of the components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine advertisements, site text (e.g., 'book online at www.hotels.com'), and site content to see whether the public would understand the term as naming the service rather than indicating source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate entirety of record under the applicable evidentiary standard
rubrics_metrics.description: On balance, the Board may give controlling weight to multiple lines of evidence (definitions, third-party usage, consumer understanding) to meet its burden; appellate review asks whether substantial evidence supports that conclusion given the heightened burden where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate and weigh dictionary definitions, third-party use, advertising, survey and declaration evidence; consider Doctrinal rules and precedent (In re STEELBUILDING.COM; Anderson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey interpretation caution: domain names may be automatically equated with brands
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers may conflate a domain name with a brand name, so survey questions that fail to reflect this nuance can produce misleadingly favorable results for applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design survey instruments to distinguish brand-perception from mere recognition of domain-name format; anticipate and counter the TTAB's skepticism that respondents equate '.com' with brand indicators (TTAB skepticism of DuPont survey).
